strengths: Introduces a novel, highly relevant threat model (Erasure Evasion Backdoors) that exposes a critical blind spot in modern concept erasure and unlearning literature for text-to-image models.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation spanning three distinct tasks (celebrity, object, and explicit content erasure), six unlearning methods (both standard and adversarially robust), and three model architectures (Stable Diffusion v1.4, v2.1, and FLUX.1).
Proposes a well-designed, score-level backdoor injection method (EEB_deep) using self-distillation, which is shown to be highly persistent across different erasure techniques.
Excellent presentation, clear figures, and thorough supplementary material detailing hyperparameter sensitivities, trigger analyses, and computational runtimes.
weaknesses: The practical motivation of the threat model could be clarified further. Since open-source poisoned models are already functional, an adversary who wants to generate harmful content could simply use the pre-erased or un-erased model. The paper would benefit from a more detailed discussion on why downstream defenders would choose to sanitize untrusted open-source checkpoints rather than clean official checkpoints.

While the paper successfully identifies the vulnerability and explores detection methods, it does not propose a concrete unlearning-time defense or mitigation strategy that successfully removes the backdoor trigger along with the target concept without degrading model utility.

strengths: The paper introduces a highly novel and timely security perspective on concept erasure in text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models: the Erasure Evasion Backdoor (EEB), demonstrating how pre-existing backdoors can survive subsequent sanitization/unlearning.

The authors formulate a comprehensive set of threat models spanning black-box data poisoning (EEBdata) to deep white-box score-based distillation (EEBdeep), showing that deeper interventions yield significantly higher persistence against robust erasure methods.

The experimental evaluation is highly thorough, testing against six state-of-the-art concept erasure techniques (both standard and adversarially robust ones) across multiple domains (celebrities, objects, and explicit content).

The work demonstrates impressive generalization across different architectures, showing that the vulnerability is not U-Net specific and successfully translates to modern rectified-flow Transformer models like FLUX.
The paper is exceptionally well-written, with clear explanations of the math, intuitive figures, and well-designed tables that support the core claims.
weaknesses: The suggested countermeasures and remedies are primarily diagnostic (weight-anomaly and activation monitoring at inference time) rather than showing a proactive or modified unlearning algorithm that can robustly eliminate these deep latent shortcuts during the erasure stage.

The computational overhead of injecting the deep backdoor (EEBdeep takes 2.5 GPU hours) is relatively high compared to the lightweight closed-form edits, although still highly practical for an adversary.

strengths: The paper introduces a highly novel and realistic threat model (Erasure Evasion Backdoors, EEB) where an adversary poisons a text-to-image diffusion model so that subsequent concept erasure fails to remove access to harmful concepts when triggered.

The paper provides a comprehensive and rigorous evaluation across six concept erasure methods (including three advanced robust unlearning methods: RECE, RECELER, and ADVUNLEARN) and three distinct tasks (celebrity identity, object erasure, and explicit content).
Great architectural generalization, with successful demonstrations on Stable Diffusion v1.4, SD v2.1, and the modern DiT-based FLUX architecture.
The work is well-structured and thoroughly analyzed, including detailed ablation studies on the loss components, trigger choices, trajectory analysis, and detection feasibility.
weaknesses: The proposed remedies and defenses are somewhat limited. While the paper demonstrates that backdoors can be detected via activation monitoring or spectral analysis, it does not provide a robust unlearning/erasure method that successfully neutralizes both the target concept and its backdoor triggers without degrading general utility.

While the threat model is highly compelling, the conceptual idea of exploiting backdoors to evade unlearning has been studied in traditional classification networks. The novelty lies in the execution and adaptation to the complex denoising process of diffusion models, but the overarching security paradigm is evolutionary.

The training details for EEBdeep involve multiple hyperparameters (such as the interpolation weight alpha and various prompt templates) that might require tedious tuning depending on the target concept, and the scalability to a larger number of parallel concepts could be further explored.
